content: 1. Gemifloxacin, like other fluoroquinolones, is associated with an increased risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture across all age groups. 2. The Achilles tendon is most commonly affected, and ruptures in this tendon may require surgical intervention. 3. Tendinitis and tendon ruptures have also been reported in other areas, including the rotator cuff (shoulder), hand, biceps, thumb, and other tendon sites. 4. The risk of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis and tendon rupture is higher in patients over 60 years of age, those taking corticosteroids, and individuals with kidney, heart, or lung transplants. 5. Additional factors that may independently increase the risk of tendon rupture include strenuous physical activity, renal failure, and pre-existing tendon disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis. 6. Tendinitis and tendon rupture have also occurred in patients without these risk factors. 7. Tendon rupture can occur during or after therapy, with cases reported several months after treatment completion. 8. Gemifloxacin should be discontinued if a patient experiences pain, swelling, inflammation, or tendon rupture. 9. Patients should rest at the first sign of tendinitis or tendon rupture and consult their healthcare provider about switching to a non-quinolone antimicrobial drug. 10. The safety and effectiveness of gemifloxacin in children, adolescents under 18 years, pregnant women, and lactating women have not been established. 11. Fluoroquinolones, including gemifloxacin, may prolong the QT interval in some patients. 12. Pharmacokinetic studies between gemifloxacin and drugs that prolong the QTc interval, such as erythromycin, antipsychotics, and tricyclic antidepressants, have not been conducted. 13. Gemifloxacin should be used cautiously when co-administered with these drugs or in patients with proarrhythmic conditions, such as significant bradycardia or acute myocardial ischemia. 14. No cardiovascular morbidity or mortality attributable to QTc prolongation was observed in over 8,119 patients treated with gemifloxacin, including 707 patients concurrently receiving QTc-prolonging drugs and 7 patients with hypokalemia. 15. The likelihood of QTc prolongation increases with higher doses of the drug; therefore, the recommended dose should not be exceeded, especially in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 16. QTc prolongation may increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes. 17. The maximal change in the QTc interval occurs approximately 5-10 hours after oral administration of gemifloxacin. 18. Serious hypersensitivity and/or anaphylactic reactions have been reported in patients receiving fluoroquinolone therapy, including gemifloxacin. 19. Hypersensitivity reactions may occur after the first dose and have occasionally been fatal. 20. These reactions may include cardiovascular collapse, hypotension/shock, seizures, loss of consciousness, tingling, angioedema (e.g., tongue, laryngeal, throat, or facial swelling), airway obstruction (e.g., bronchospasm, shortness of breath, acute respiratory distress), dyspnea, urticaria, itching, and other severe skin reactions. 21. Gemifloxacin should be discontinued immediately at the first sign of a hypersensitivity reaction, such as a skin rash or other manifestations. 22. Serious acute hypersensitivity reactions may require treatment with epinephrine and other resuscitative measures, including oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management as clinically indicated. 23. Other serious and sometimes fatal events, some due to hypersensitivity and others of uncertain etiology, have been reported rarely in patients receiving quinolones, including gemifloxacin. 24. These events may include toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, vasculitis, arthralgia, myalgia, serum sickness, allergic pneumonitis, interstitial nephritis, acute renal insufficiency or failure, hepatitis, jaundice, acute hepatic necrosis or failure, anemia (including hemolytic and aplastic), thrombocytopenia (including thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), leukopenia, agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, and other hematologic abnormalities. 25. Gemifloxacin should be discontinued immediately at the first appearance of a skin rash, jaundice, or any other sign of hypersensitivity, and supportive measures should be instituted. 26. Rare cases of sensory or sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy affecting small and/or large axons, resulting in paresthesias, hypoesthesias, dysesthesias, and weakness, have been reported in patients receiving quinolones. 27. Central nervous system (CNS) effects have been infrequently reported in clinical studies with gemifloxacin. 28. Gemifloxacin should be used cautiously in patients with CNS diseases such as epilepsy or those predisposed to seizures. 29. Although not observed in gemifloxacin clinical trials, seizures, increased intracranial pressure, and toxic psychosis have been reported in patients receiving other fluoroquinolones. 30. CNS stimulation caused by fluoroquinolones may lead to tremors, restlessness, anxiety, lightheadedness, confusion, hallucinations, paranoia, depression, insomnia, and, rarely, suicidal thoughts or actions. 31. If these reactions occur in patients receiving gemifloxacin, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate measures should be taken. 32. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including gemifloxacin, and may range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. 33. Antibacterial treatment alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile. 34. C. difficile produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. 35. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. 36. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. 37. A thorough medical history is necessary, as CDAD has been reported to occur over two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. 38. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. 39. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated.
